text: A government decides that its oldest citizens cost more than they return, and builds a colony to keep them in. Teca is seventy-seven, living in the Amazon village of Muriti, when the qualifying age drops far enough to include her. What follows is a run downriver: boats, back channels, whatever underworld will carry a woman who is not supposed to be travelling. Gabriel Mascaro allows eighty-six minutes for it. The science fiction is administrative rather than technological, a Brazil that looks like the one outside the window with a single law added, and the pressure comes from how plausible the paperwork feels. Set against that machinery, what Teca wants is almost weightless: she has never been on a plane, and would like to be. It carries a Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize.

The soliloquy everyone knows is delivered here with the actor's back turned to the camera. That choice is a fair index of how Grigori Kozintsev approached the play in 1964: in Russian, in a real castle in Estonia, with the stone standing in for the enclosure Hamlet has to think his way out of before he can act on his father's death. Venice gave it a Grand Jury Prize. A hundred and forty minutes, and the court around the prince is all appetite, drink and celebration, while Innokenti Smoktunovsky plays the one man in the room listening to himself. Purists had plenty to object to. The speech goes unillustrated, and the audience is left to supply what a man means when nobody can see his mouth move.

The building is a psychiatric hospital on the border between Russia and Chechnya, and it gets invaded twice. Venice gave Andrei Konchalovsky its Grand Jury Prize for what he does with that arrangement, which is mostly to decline the war film it could have been. The patients have illnesses to manage and days to fill. Soldiers arrive with their own arrangements to make, and the institution absorbs both. A hundred and four minutes, in Russian, produced out of France, and romance sits in the genre list beside war, which is not decoration: the current that carries most of the film runs through people the fighting would not think to count. The organising unit is the ward rather than the battle, and the war enters as men with rifles and questions about who the place belongs to.

A man is hurt at work, and the operation that repairs him turns him into public property. Jacek was a metalhead with a job and an appetite for a good night; afterwards he is the first person in Poland to receive a face transplant, and the country needs him to be a miracle, a martyr, a story television can run. The film holds a Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize. Małgorzata Szumowska keeps it to ninety-one minutes and lets comedy carry most of the weight, which is the tell: the pity gathering around Jacek is broader and colder than the accident ever was. Attention on that scale arrives with conditions attached, and none of them were negotiated. What he stands to lose is not the face. It is the right to decide what the face is going to mean.

A man who spends his working life inside very small mechanisms is told by the police that his son has killed someone. Michel Descombes repairs watches in Lyons and lives alone with Bernard, a teenager who is now on the run with a girl. Bertrand Tavernier gives the crime almost none of the screen: the boy is gone, the facts arrive secondhand, and what is left is a father reassembling a person he thought he had raised. A hundred and five minutes, 1974, filed under thriller and crime although the suspense is entirely domestic. It took the Louis Delluc Prize and a Golden Bear. Most of the work happens in ordinary rooms, where a quiet man is asked questions about someone he loves and finds he cannot answer them.

Three German soldiers are posted to a small coastal community on Kos while one of them, Stroszek, heals, and the war carries on without them. There is nothing to do. That is the premise and, across ninety-one minutes, close to the whole substance of it: heat, a uniform with no function attached, days that will not fill themselves. Werner Herzog made it in 1968, and it took German Film Awards for direction and for the feature itself, along with a Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize. Idleness is handled here as a physical force with weight and direction rather than as a mood, and the film is willing to spend real time proving the point. Occupation without occupation is a strange thing to put three armed men through.

Hollywood, seen from Alexandria in wartime, is not entertainment but a plan. Yehia is eighteen and certain his life is meant to happen in America, at a film school, at a distance from the dying and the shortage the Second World War has brought to his city. The obstacles are money and a middle-class family's idea of what a son does. A Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize came out of Berlin for it, and it was entered for the Academy Awards. Youssef Chahine takes a hundred and thirty-three minutes, in Arabic, and gives the daydreams their full running length instead of mocking them. What the film weighs is the price of wanting a life assembled somewhere else, in a borrowed language, on the far side of a war.

The job is to watch the monitors after the supermarket closes, which mostly means watching nobody. Then there is somebody: a woman on the late cleaning shift, and a guard who starts arranging his attention around her. Berlin gave it a Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize. Adrián Biniez keeps to eighty-eight minutes, in Spanish, and everything turns on distance, on how long a man can look at someone through a screen before looking becomes something he has to do in person. Romance is the second genre listed, and the film has to earn that word against a premise which, stated flatly, is surveillance. The comedy and the discomfort come from one source. What has to be settled, minute by minute, is how near attention sits to intrusion.

The priest whose parish Giulio takes over left the clergy to start a family. Giulio arrives in Rome young and ordained and glad to be home among his mother, his sister and the friends he grew up with, and finds that those friends were radicals once and are now each managing the aftermath of a defeat in their own way. Nanni Moretti runs ninety-four minutes on that arrangement. The pattern that emerges is quietly punishing: a man whose whole office is to help is surrounded by people whose trouble has moved beyond the reach of help, and he keeps offering anyway. Italy gave it a David di Donatello for direction, Berlin a Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize. What it follows is a son, a brother and a friend who happens to be a priest.

One hundred and sixty-five minutes long, and almost none of that is plot. Sergei comes back from the army, takes a job at a thermal power station and falls in again with the friends he grew up with: Slava, who has a young family, and Nikolai, who is good company. On a bus he sees a woman, and that is that. Marlen Khutsiyev is filming a generation at the moment it begins testing what it was handed, the principles and the traditions and the received account of how a life is supposed to go, and he does it by letting an ordinary week run at close to its real length. An evening, a shift and a conversation are events of equal size here. The Soviet Union, 1965. Venice gave it a Grand Jury Prize.

Two couples see each other constantly, and one afternoon rearranges all four of them. Christian talks on a small radio station, his wife Katrin directs cars in a car park, their friend Uwe runs a fast-food kiosk and Ellen sells perfume. The lives are narrow and settled, and the film takes that as material rather than as a verdict. Then Chris and Ellen sleep together, and everything the four had agreed not to examine comes up for examination. Andreas Dresen holds it at a hundred and eleven minutes and never asks these jobs to stand for anything larger. The European Film Awards gave him their directing prize, and their audience prize went the same way. Whatever breaks here has to be repaired by the same four people, with the same shifts to work on Monday.

A novelist goes to see a colleague who stopped answering, and the day keeps handing her other people. A bookstore, then a walk with a film director and his wife, then an actress, and out of that a proposal: the two of them should make something together. Ninety-two minutes, and the largest event available is that proposal. Hong Sang-soo builds the whole of it out of meetings and the talk inside them, so the stakes run exactly as far as what two people can say to each other before one of them has to leave. Berlin gave it a Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize and Korean critics added an award of their own. The interest is in the accumulating record of who says what, to whom, and how much of it is meant at the time.

The Hotel Europa is expecting diplomats on 28 June 2014, a hundred years to the day after the shooting that is said to have started the First World War. Upstairs, in a sealed suite, a guest from France rehearses an appeal for peace. Downstairs the staff have gone months without pay: Hatidza, from the laundry, has just been elected to lead a strike, and her daughter Lamija, on reception, is against it. Danis Tanović stacks the building floor by floor like an argument, and keeps a television reporter working the same day on whether Gavrilo Princip was a criminal or a hero. Eighty-five minutes. The ceremony above needs the century to mean one thing; the people holding the hotel together need to be paid this week.

In 2008, death-squad killings in Hungary took several Roma families in their homes. Benedek Fliegauf made this four years afterwards and set it inside one family that is planning to leave the country. Ninety-eight minutes, in Hungarian, produced out of Germany. Horror is the right word for it in the oldest sense, the one concerned with who is allowed to feel safe indoors. The dread is structural rather than staged: everyone in the house knows what has been happening in the district, and the day proceeds anyway, through work and school and the ordinary sequence of errands a family runs while it arranges an exit. It took a Lux Prize and a Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize. The family is never handled as a case study. They are people with somewhere to be.
